opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. In AML, the core problem is that the space of possible drug combinations is enormous, and every patient's tumor is molecularly different. We can measure gene expression across thousands of genes for each patient sample, and we have ex vivo drug response data, but the number of samples is small relative to the number of features. So a model that just outputs "this combination will be synergistic" isn't enough. Clinicians and biologists won't trust it, and frankly they shouldn't, unless they can see why.

That's where explanations come in. In our work we trained ensembles of tree-based models to predict drug synergy from the expression profiles of the patient's cancer and features of the drugs, and then used Shapley-value-based attributions to ask which genes drive a given prediction. What turned out to be really valuable is that the explanations aren't just a sanity check. They're scientific output in their own right. When we aggregated attributions across many patients and drug pairs, a coherent biological signal came out. For example, genes associated with hematopoietic differentiation, a more stem-like versus more differentiated state of the leukemia cells, kept showing up as major drivers of whether certain combinations would work. That gives you a hypothesis about mechanism, and a potential biomarker for choosing which patients should get which combination.

There's also a subtlety we had to deal with. Gene expression data is highly correlated, so if you naively explain a single model, the attribution can land somewhat arbitrarily on one gene versus its correlated neighbors. Using ensembles and looking at robust, aggregated explanations helped us get attributions that reflect real biology rather than artifacts of a particular fit.

So the bigger picture is this: in a high-stakes, data-limited domain like cancer treatment, accuracy alone doesn't get you to the clinic. Explanations let you validate the model against known biology, discover new biology, and ultimately give a clinician a rationale they can act on for an individual patient. That's why I see explainability not as an add-on but as central to making machine learning useful for precision oncology.

r003.rationale: It describes models predicting drug synergy using patient cancer expression profiles and features of the drugs.

r004.rationale: It says SHAP-based attributions identify which genes drive a given prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the AML work is a good example of why I think explainability isn't just a nice-to-have in biomedicine, it's actually the point.

The setup is this: we have patient samples, bone marrow or blood from people with acute myeloid leukemia, and we can measure a lot about each one, gene expression, mutations, and so on. We also have ex vivo drug sensitivity data, where you expose the patient's cells to a panel of drugs and see what kills them. The obvious machine learning question is, can we predict which drug a given patient will respond to? And you can build a model that does that reasonably well.

But here's the problem. If I give a clinician a black box that says "patient X will respond to drug A," that's not very actionable on its own, and it's definitely not something you can design a combination around. Combinations are where the real therapeutic leverage is in AML, because resistance to single agents is so common. And the space of possible combinations is enormous. You can't just screen all of them, and you certainly can't run clinical trials on all of them.

So what we did is use explanation methods, things like SHAP, to ask the model not just "what will happen" but "why." Which genes or pathways is the model relying on when it predicts sensitivity or resistance to a particular drug? And when you do that across many drugs, you start to see structure. You see that drug A's predicted efficacy depends on one set of biological features, and drug B's depends on a different, sometimes complementary set. That gives you a hypothesis: if these two drugs are exploiting different vulnerabilities in the same patient, combining them might be synergistic, or might overcome the resistance mechanism the model is flagging for one of them.

What I really like about this is that it turns the model into a hypothesis-generating tool rather than just a predictor. The explanations are something a cancer biologist can look at and say, "Oh, that's interesting, that pathway makes sense," or "That's surprising, let's go test it." And in fact, when we took some of those explanation-derived combinations into the lab, we saw synergy that we would not have found by brute-force screening in any reasonable amount of time.

The broader point for me is that in biology and medicine, the prediction is rarely the final deliverable. What people actually want is understanding, mechanism, something they can act on and build on. Explainable models let the ML be part of the scientific conversation instead of a separate oracle off to the side.

r001.rationale: The response says drugs that exploit different, complementary biological features in the same patient might be synergistic.

r002.rationale: It discusses patient samples and genomic measurements but does not state that genomic differences make patients with the same cancer respond differently to the same drugs.

r003.rationale: It describes predicting individual drug response from patient data, not predicting drug synergy using gene expression and candidate drug information as inputs.

r004.rationale: Explanations are said to show features behind predicted drug sensitivity or resistance, but not features supporting a predicted drug synergy.

r005.rationale: It describes finding structure across explanations for many drugs, not analyzing SHAP explanations across drug combinations to discover a general principle of synergy.

r006.rationale: It does not mention pairing drugs targeting less differentiated and more differentiated cancer.

astra-6.text:
When we’re choosing a combination of cancer drugs, we want to understand more than whether a model predicts that it will work. We want to understand why it makes that prediction. Which characteristics of the leukemia cells are driving it, and what might those characteristics tell us about vulnerabilities we could target together?

That’s where explanations can be valuable. Two drugs could receive similar predictions but for different reasons. Understanding those differences can help us formulate hypotheses about which combinations might be complementary and which patients might benefit. There are so many possible combinations that we can’t test everything, so that guidance matters.

Of course, an explanation of a model isn’t proof of a biological mechanism. It gives us a hypothesis to investigate experimentally. The value is in connecting the prediction to biological questions that can guide the next experiment.

r001.rationale: The response mentions hypotheses about complementary combinations, but does not explain that targeting complementary biological pathways can produce drug synergy.

r002.rationale: It says some patients might benefit, but does not state that genomic differences cause patients with the same cancer type to respond differently to the same drugs.

r003.rationale: It discusses model predictions generally, without formulating a machine learning task or naming gene expression and candidate-drug information as inputs.

r004.rationale: It says leukemia-cell characteristics may drive a prediction, but does not identify gene-expression features as supporting a predicted drug synergy.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention SHAP, analyzing explanations across many combinations, or deriving a general principle of drug synergy.

r006.rationale: It does not describe pairing drugs targeting less- and more-differentiated cancer.

sol-6.1.text:
In acute myeloid leukemia, different patients can respond very differently to the same treatment. A model might predict that a particular drug will work, but for choosing a combination, we want to understand why it makes that prediction. Which molecular features is it using, and what might those features tell us about the cancer’s vulnerabilities?

Explanations can help us turn a prediction into a biological hypothesis. If we can identify potentially complementary vulnerabilities, we can propose drug combinations to test experimentally. The explanation doesn’t establish that a combination will work, but it can help us prioritize experiments in a very large space of possible combinations.

r001.rationale: It mentions potentially complementary vulnerabilities and proposing combinations, but does not state that targeting complementary biological pathways produces drug synergy.

r002.rationale: It says patients can respond differently to the same treatment, but does not attribute this to genomic differences.

r003.rationale: It does not formulate synergy prediction as a machine learning task or specify gene expression and candidate-drug information as inputs.

r004.rationale: It says explanations can show which molecular features a model uses, but does not connect patient gene-expression features to a predicted drug synergy.

r005.rationale: It does not describe SHAP analysis across combinations or a general principle discovered from such analysis.

r006.rationale: It does not identify a pairing of drugs targeting less differentiated and more differentiated cancer.
